extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for forming, testing, and interpreting inductive generalizations and causal claims; focuses on what counts as a cause, how inductions corroborate or conflict, and what guarantees universality. Useful for evaluating the legitimacy and strength of causal inferences in scientific and philosophical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductions strengthened by deduction from stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction that can be shown to be a corollary or deduction from stronger, better-established inductions acquires the strength of those inductions (and may even gain additional strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine weaker historical or empirical generalizations with more general, better-established facts to raise their certainty; example: a historical generalization about abuse of power is more certain when shown to follow from established facts about average human character and ineffective education. Torricellian experiment strengthened constituent laws (e.g., weight of the atmosphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority to stronger inductions in case of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When an induction conflicts with stronger inductions or their deductive consequences, the weaker induction must yield unless the stronger one is shown to be overgeneralized beyond its evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inconsistency with well-established scientific truths to reject or revise weaker, insufficient inductions (e.g., superstitions rejected by subsequent scientific knowledge). Reconsider universality claims of stronger inductions only when evidence warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual confirmation among connectable inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions that can be connected by ratiocination (deduction) confirm one another; a conclusion deduced from several inductions rises at least to the certainty of the weakest premise and generally increases overall certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where inductions are logically linked, use their deductive relations as confirmatory evidence (illustrated by combining several laws to derive Kepler-like results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/geometrical laws as standards of rigorous universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of number and space (arithmetic and geometry) are the paradigms of certainty and universality against which other uniformities are compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that geometry and arithmetic are laws of simultaneity or number and do not by themselves yield laws of succession; they are premises that can help deduce succession only when combined with genuine laws of succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of laws of succession for inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer future events or establish causal laws you need fundamental laws of succession (not just laws of number/space); such laws must be indefeasible within their domain to serve as foundations for other inductive inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a law of succession co-extensive with successive phenomena (the Law of Causation) to form reliable inductive procedures; avoid attempts to derive temporal regularities solely from spatial/mathematical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Universal Causation (every beginning has a cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every phenomenon that has a beginning is preceded by some antecedent or set of antecedents on which it is invariably consequent; this universality underlies the possibility of inductive logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the belief that every event depends on some law as central to searching for causal explanations; use it as justification that if we can discover the antecedent combination, we can predict or explain the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as physical antecedent(s) (not metaphysical/efficient causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive logic, 'cause' denotes physical antecedents—phenomena observable in experience—not metaphysical 'efficient' causes or ultimate ontological explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit causal inquiry to empirical antecedents and regular antecedent-consequent relations; avoid metaphysical speculations about 'ultimate' causes when constructing inductive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as the whole conjunction of conditions (positive and negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophically, the cause of a phenomenon is the sum total of all positive and negative conditions whose concurrence invariably produces the effect; singling out one condition as 'the cause' is often a convenience, not scientific accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specifying causes, aim (where accuracy matters) to enumerate all relevant conditions or acknowledge implicit ones; examples: death after eating depends on food plus constitution, health state, atmosphere, etc.; saying 'the food caused death' is a shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarely single-factor causation; complex conjunctive antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation is seldom a relation between a consequent and a single antecedent; it typically involves the concurrence of multiple antecedents, where one may be highlighted as the proximate event but is not the sole operative condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and identify combinations of antecedents (conjunctive causes); beware attributing causation to the most conspicuous antecedent without testing for other necessary conditions (e.g., exposure plus particular constitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical naming of causes vs conditions (convenience vs completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary language often names the proximate or most conspicuous condition as 'the cause' while omitting other necessary conditions; this is permissible for many purposes but scientifically incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between colloquial causal attributions (for emphasis or responsibility) and complete scientific statements that list all indispensable conditions; footnote omitted conditions when precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative conditions summarized as absence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative conditions (absences) that are required for an effect can generally be summarized as the absence of preventing or counteracting causes, allowing one to limit the notion of cause to positive antecedents plus a common negative-condition assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In causal accounts, it is acceptable to omit detailed negative conditions by assuming absence of counteracting forces, provided this universal negative condition is understood; e.g., gravity's effects assume no stronger counteracting forces present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent vs patient distinction is not fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: The common distinction between an active 'agent' cause and a passive 'patient' is largely verbal; what are called 'patients' often function as agents or active contributors to effects and should be considered among the conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reifying an agent/patient dichotomy in causal analysis; include properties of the 'patient' (e.g., organism constitution) among the causal factors rather than treating them as mere passive background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation can produce dispositions or states of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes often produce capacities or properties in objects (states of preparation) that make them capable of producing other effects later; such dispositions count as effects of prior causes and as antecedents for subsequent effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing causal chains, include intermediate dispositional states (e.g., gunpowder becoming explosive, a wall acquiring paint) as legitimate causal outcomes; recognize that these are often permanent or long-lasting conditions for later events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation implies belief in future invariability under current constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining a cause as an antecedent that 'invariably precedes' a consequent requires not merely past regularity but the judgment that, given the current constitution of things, the antecedent will continue to produce the consequent in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate causal claims that rest on observed past succession from those justified by expectation of continued regularity; use this criterion to reject mere historically regular sequences that lack grounding in enduring conditions (e.g., day causing night is not causal in this sense).
